item.title: A local’s travel guide to Austin: what to eat, see and do in three days
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Pre-analysis score: 1.54
Standout spots include food truck parks, honky-tonk hangouts and Lady Bird’s wildflower sanctuary From phone chargers to podcasts, the best road trip accessories make the miles fly by Austin has become one of the most popular places in the US to move to, and also to visit. Droves of people descend on the city in March for the South by Southwest tech, film and music festival and in the fall for the Austin City Limits music festival. And Austin is one of the top five destinations in the US for bachelorette parties. Don’t let the bachelorettes scare you away, though. Austin is a great place to spend a few days, so long as you do it like a local. My family and I moved to Austin 12 years ago, after living in New York for many years. I’ve also lived in Washington DC , the San Francisco Bay Area and Philadelphia. Austin has a feel all of its own: it has a world-class music scene, great food that now goes well beyond Tex-Mex and barbecue, Texas history and fun shopping and museums – all with less hassle than bigger cities in the US. item.title: A local’s travel guide to Washington DC: what to eat, see and do in three days
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Pre-analysis score: 1.54
Top sights in Washington include Capitol Hill Books, the Black Cat music venue and a top-rated Filipino restaurant From phone chargers to podcasts, the best road trip accessories make the miles fly by People love to be rude about Washington DC because it’s full of so many politicians, feds, and consultants who wear fleece vests and don’t take off their work lanyards when they leave the office. I get it. I myself had mixed feelings about my home town when I was growing up there. It didn’t seem as exciting as New York, or as glitzy as Los Angeles. But after a decade away, I came back, because time is circular, and also it turns out DC rocks and I love it! It has great restaurants, resplendent parks and free museums. Sometimes when I’m sad I’ll put on red lipstick and go wander around the National Gallery of Art for an afternoon, staring at gorgeous paintings and sulking in a way that I hope looks beautiful and intriguing to strangers. item.title: Building a new PC from old parts? Don’t reuse these components
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
When building a new desktop computer, it makes sense to reuse as many components as possible from your old machine. That very flexibility is one of the greatest advantages of a self-built system! Nevertheless, it is worth exercising caution here: some components age without you realizing it, or are no longer technically compatible with modern hardware. Anyone putting together a new PC should carefully check which parts should really be reused. The power supply is particularly critical. Whilst many users continue to use a high-quality model across several generations of computers, electronic components do age. Capacitors lose performance over time, and new graphics cards or processors may have higher or different power requirements. Fitting a new PC with old parts from its predecessor sounds tempting, but is not always advisable – for example, in the case of second-hand memory modules. Newegg You should therefore check the age, power rating and condition of the power supply unit before installation. If the unit is already many years old or offers only a small power reserve, replacing it is usually the safer option. A common and potentially dangerous mistake concerns modular power supply cables. Even if the plugs look identical, the pin configurations often differ between different power supply models. Connecting old cables to a new power supply can lead to short circuits. Therefore, when replacing the power supply, always use only the cables supplied with the specific model. Older hard drives and SSDs should also be assessed carefully. When it comes to RAM, modules with different specifications can be used together. However, the overall performance depends on the weakest link. Kingston Mechanical hard drives are subject to wear and tear due to their moving parts, whilst early SSD models often have significantly lower write endurance than current flash memory drives. Such storage devices can still serve as a secondary drive or for less important data, but should, where possible, no longer be used as the system drive. The same applies to mixed or very old RAM modules. Although different memory modules often work together, stability and speed are always determined by the weakest module. For a new PC, a uniform RAM kit is therefore usually recommended. The power supply unit is often used across several generations of PCs. In particular, the capacitors age over time and lose performance. It is therefore often advisable to replace them. Foundry Old all-in-one water-cooling systems also warrant attention. The integrated pump has a limited lifespan and may lose performance or even fail over the years. Modern air coolers now also achieve very good results and are often the more reliable choice in the long term. As a rule of thumb: please only carry over components if their condition, age and performance are still suitable for the new system. You should check the power supply, cables, storage drives, and cooling system particularly carefully to avoid subsequent problems or damage to new hardware.

item.title: Kensington Triple 4K TB5 dock review: Killer speeds, but a few glitches
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Affordable for a Thunderbolt 5 dock Fastest performance in some tests Two HDMI ports saves on cable cost Ports are clearly labeled 140W laptop charging Lock options Cons Stable on a TB5 laptop; varied significantly on TB4 Ports spaced a bit close together Our Verdict Kensington’s Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station (SD5010T5) is an attractively priced 13-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 dock, with excellent performance but questionable stability. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $299.99 Best Prices Today: Kensington SD5010T5 EQ Thunderbolt 5 Dock Retailer Price $296.49 View Deal Kensington $299.99 View Deal $304.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Kensington’s Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station (SD5010T5, sometimes referred to as the SD5010T5 EQ) feels like a 13-in-1 Thunderbolt 5 dock for the PC, rather than the Mac, with multiple HDMI ports rather than a host of Thunderbolt upstream connections. Performance is stellar; stability, less so. In 2026, a Thunderbolt 5 dock probably shouldn’t be your first choice, precisely because Thunderbolt 5 host support is limited to a few gaming laptops like the Asus ROG Strix, which served as my testbed for this review. Nevertheless, my list of the best Thunderbolt docks includes both Thunderbolt 4 and Thunderbolt 5 offerings, precisely because of the willingness of manufacturers to keep pricing in check. At about $300, Kensington’s dock is priced roughly in line with where I’d expect a TB5 dock to be. A Thunderbolt 5 dock is designed for up to three 4K displays, at 144Hz apiece, up from the two 4K60 displays that Thunderbolt 4 supports. Alternatively, you can connect a pair of 6K displays, or one running at 8K resolution. Through last year, TB5 was more of a performance play, for gaming. At CES 2026, however, we saw mass-market 6K displays enter the market , adding a new productivity wrinkle. Kensington Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station: Construction and ports The dock’s design is straightforward, with a small but thorough instruction sheet and small icons on the dock itself which spell out the capabilities of most of the ports themselves. Case in point: On the front, underneath the power button, a small icon notes that the 10Gbps USB-C port charges at up to 30W, enough for most of the latest smartphones to fast-charge. The 10Gbps USB-C port next to it is a bit more vague, with a battery icon. It too provides power, but just 7.5W. The USB-A port to the right also provides 10Gbps of throughput, but just 4.5W, which is normal. This dock includes what Kensington calls KonstantCharge, which will keep the peripheral ports active and charging even when there’s no laptop connected. That function worked as advertised. Mark Hachman / Foundry There are also two Thunderbolt ports on the rear of the dock. The first, which serves as an additional display port, only supplies 15W, somewhat surprisingly low for a Thunderbolt 5 port. Next to it are a pair of HDMI 2.1 ports. Above are a pair of 5Gbps USB-A ports, a 2.5Gbps Ethernet connection, and a pair of Kensington locking ports, nano and standard. I rarely complain about the port spacing on a powered desktop dock, but here I feel that the spacing between the two Thunderbolt ports on the rear of the dock — the connection to the laptop, and then the additional Thunderbolt 5 connection — are too close together. It’s not impossible to manage, but with those and the Ethernet cable in close proximity, inserting and withdrawing a cable has to be fiddled with. A wider, rectangular dock usually doesn’t have this problem. The second Thunderbolt 5 port supplies 140W to the attached laptop. That’s a problem — and will always be a problem, since gaming laptops with Thunderbolt 5 connections generally require 200W or so under load, including gaming. On the other hand, while my test laptop did complain of a “slow charger,” the laptop only lost about 4 percent of its battery while connected over the course of an afternoon’s worth of work. Put another way, the power that most TB5 docks provide will be insufficient for the Windows laptops which can connect to them, but not dramatically so. Dock makers have told me that placing wireless charging into the top of the dock can cause crosstalk and noise that can interfere with signaling. Still, there’s a lot of unused surface space, which mounting the dock can get around. Otherwise, the top of the dock became what I would call hot to the touch. There’s no active cooling, so that surface area is used to dissipate heat. Mark Hachman / Foundry I tend to favor vertical docks, because they can provide additional space savings on a crowded desk. However, Kensington’s 13-in-1 TB5 aluminum dock is incredibly sturdy and secure, with a rubberized surface that covers the entirety of the underside and prevents it from being moved or dragged by the weight of the attached cables. It can even be mounted via a pair of screw holes on the bottom, too. (For a Mac-specific perspective on the Kensington SD501T5, see Macworld’s review .) Kensington Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station: Performance I usually test docks over a period of several days, using our methodology for testing Thunderbolt docks , to assess how stable they are. Does the dock light up the displays when it comes back from sleep? Are there issues with it disconnecting? My test laptop produced a BSOD on one occasion following a graphical glitch on one display when it resumed from sleep, which may have been due to the laptop rather than the docking station itself. After a reboot, one of the displays failed to light up until after I reconnected it. My stability testing varied dramatically. On my Thunderbolt 5 test bed, the dock was extremely stable. On a laptop with Thunderbolt 4 ports, however, I noticed that one of two displays didn’t resume after bringing the laptop back from sleep. A reboot solved this. More annoyingly, one of the displays would flip off for a second or two, every few minutes. I tried six different Thunderbolt 4 laptops; three demonstrated this problem, while the other three did not. Otherwise, two displays lit up at 4K/144Hz, as they should, and the dock powered a third display that I connected with a USB-C cable. (It’s worth noting that the Kensington Dockworks software can be downloaded and installed, though it’s more for management rather than stability — quicker switching from Ethernet to Wi-Fi if the connection shifts, for example.) In my tests using a USB voltage meter, I found that the dock supplied 26W out of the front charging port, versus the rated 30W, but 8.1W out of the second USB-C port, versus the rated 7.5W. The other front USB-A port delivered 2.4W. Mark Hachman / Foundry As a Thunderbolt 5 dock, however, paired with capable hardware, this dock simply flies. As per my testing methodology mentioned above, I stream a 4K/60Hz video and note any frame drops. There were none! (I usually see a few frames drop.) Ditto for two displays. I then connect a Thunderbolt 5-capable external SSD to the dock and run PCMark’s external storage drive test. The only odd thing I noticed here is that the drive wouldn’t function on either of the two front-facing 10Gbps ports. It should have, just at slower speeds. On the rear Thunderbolt 5 port, it performed normally. Well, not totally normally. Using PCMark and the TB5 SSD, the dock achieved 444 megabytes per second, sneaking past the Plugable TBT-UD3 (432MB/s) as the fastest dock in that particular test. Running in the background while I was streaming the 4K video reduced the performance slightly to 439MB/s. My next test is to copy a folder full of multimedia files from the drive, through the dock, and on to my PC’s desktop. Last year’s Sonnet Echo 13 holds the crown at 13.9 seconds to complete the task. This took a few seconds longer, at 18.7 seconds, a 30 percent difference. I can remember the days when I would get a cup of coffee while my PC booted; five seconds or so isn’t a huge difference, but it is significant. While streaming and copying, the process took 20.2 seconds. Should you buy the Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station? Great performance, iffy stability — at least on my tests of Thunderbolt 4 hardware. I’m always a fan of display ports, as it means that you won’t need to buy adapter cables. That’s a not-so-hidden gotcha of docks like the Plugable TBT-UD3, which simply includes Thunderbolt ports instead. Tack on a couple of cables to the Plugable’s $250 price, and you’re inside the $300 price of the Kensington SD5010T5. I’m going to have to do a bit of thinking on whether I include this dock among my recommended best picks for Thunderbolt docking stations , which already include some Kensington docks. Kensington’s Thunderbolt 5 Triple 4K Docking Station is a solid dock if you already own a Thunderbolt 5 laptop; otherwise, the possible stability issues on a Thunderbolt 4 laptop might prove annoying.

item.title: My robot vacuum can map a house. My car broke its brain
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
So let me set the scene here. It’s Friday afternoon, and I’m picking up a few friends for a Taylor Swift-themed hangout later on. But the backseat of my car is covered in dog hair, and I’m in no mood to wrestle one of those long-hosed vacuums at my local car wash. The suction on those things sucks anyway. Literally. And then it dawned on me. I’ve got two robot vacuums upstairs. What would happen if I just stuck one of them in the back? Just to give you a visual here, my car is a hatchback, so it’s shorter than a sedan. I’ve also got a giant greyhound, so I tend to drive with the back seats folded flat (he needs a lot of room!). In other words, it’s a (mostly) flat area. Surely a robot could handle that? Or so I thought. First, I plopped the budget robot vacuum in the back of my car. It’s got a suction power of 20,000 Pa, which is pretty good for a budget model. (In case you’re curious, it was the Dreame D20 Air Plus ). Next, I programmed it to run in Standard mode. After it created a small map of the back of my car, it ran for about… five minutes. When the Dreame app told me it was finished cleaning, I scoffed. No way. So, I ran the robot vacuum again. But this time I turned up the suction level to maximum power. Sigh. Again, it finished in five minutes. I understand it’s a small space, but I expected the robot to spend more time cleaning the area. It’s definitely more thorough when it’s zooming about the house. I don’t think it sucked up a single strand of dog hair, either. My next plan? Trying a more advanced model with 35,000 Pa of suction. Maybe the trick here is more suction power. Uh, nope. It did worse than the budget model. First, it got stuck on a weird ledge and wouldn’t move because the wheels were lifted. It did manage to successfully map the back of my car (hilariously enough, the app labeled this area “Kitchen”), but when I tried to run it again, it got stuck on the same exact ledge. (It’s the Roborock Saros 20 , by the way). Why suction power isn’t the issue So why didn’t this work? Well, it turns out that a car is a much weirder environment for a robot vacuum than you might think. Foundry / Ashley Biancuzzo Even with the back seats folded down, my car doesn’t have one big, continuous expanse of flooring. The folded seats actually create a small hill in the middle. There’s also a few ledges at the corners where the surface drops down to the floor. This was enough to trip up the more expensive robot (the Saros 20). When one of the wheels lost contact with the ground, it stopped. That’s when I had to step in and physically move it. Unfortunately, it wasn’t able to finish a single cleaning cycle. These machines are designed to navigate predictable environments. Give them hardwood floors, furniture, a few walls, and they’re pretty good at figuring out where they can and can’t go. A car is a totally different story. I don’t think the robot vacuum can tell the difference between a raised ledge it can theoretically climb over and a step it absolutely cannot. It just sees a floor it thinks it can navigate. And when it gets that wrong, all the suction power in the world doesn’t matter. It’s also worth noting that the carpet in your car is very different from the carpet in your house. Automotive carpeting is usually flatter and more tightly constructed. It’s supposed to be more durable, able to withstand the constant friction from shoes. House carpets have more variation in terms of pile and texture–they can be softer and more flexible. That’s more of a robot vacuum’s bread and butter. That’s the lesson I took away from this ridiculous experiment. I went into this thinking suction power was the key here. It isn’t. A robot can have 20,000 Pa or 35,000 Pa, but suction is only useful if it’s cleaning an area it knows how to handle.

item.title: Meta’s $18 billion payout isn’t enough to save our kids
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
I’m not a parent, but I’m looking at the Meta settlement wondering if our kids are any safer. If you haven’t heard already, Meta agreed last Wednesday to settle a lawsuit over Facebook and Instagram’s affect on children. Brought by 47 states, Washington D.C., and several U.S. territories, the suit alleged that Meta purposely made its platforms addictive to kids, ultimately causing negative mental health outcomes like anxiety, depression, and even suicide. Four states (California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey) also alleged that Meta violated state consumer protection laws. Welcome to Safe Mode, your weekly report for pressing security and privacy news—and what steps to take next. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website ! A potential payout of $18 billion is on the table, with $12.7 billion in guaranteed payouts. The additional $5 billion will be paid if rivals YouTube and TikTok also agree to implement measures like a one-hour time limit, blocking late night access, and implementing age verification—plus pony up about $2.5 billion each. But Meta has also pledged reform for teen accounts of Facebook and Instagram. The biggest changes: automatically limiting teens to two hours of use per day across both platforms, muting notifications during school hours, and blocking usage from midnight through 6 a.m. Likes will also be hidden from view. The changes are a start. But the kids may not be all right for a while longer. For starters, these Facebook and Instagram changes are only mandated for 10 years. Meta can still serve personalized recommendations and targeted advertising too, if those features aren’t adjusted or turned off. And teens are allowed to send direct messages during school or late at night. (Meta describes this as allowing “teens to stay connected with friends and family.”) Most parents likely won’t automatically know they have to take additional steps to more fully protect their kids—that unless they actively poke at Facebook and Instagram settings and monitor account use, those teens could still be exposed to harmful material or conversations. For example: A feed with only content from followed accounts will be available to teens, but only if selected as the default. And bullying can still happen over direct messages. Meta says the new restrictions on teen accounts will release alongside existing parental management tools. Meta I’m also concerned about how Meta will ensure teens don’t circumvent these restrictions. The company doesn’t want to manage the age verification process directly. Instead, Meta is advocating for age verification to be performed by app stores. But that creates a whole new set of problems. First, the basic privacy risks: What documentation will be required for verification? Who will process the applications? Will biometrics be involved? How will all the data be stored? Who will have access to that data? And second: Will all apps in an app store have access to that data? Could a shady developer purposely target the under-18 crowd? Plus, age verification in general is a mess, and will be a mess for a while longer. Governments have begun passing legislation requiring it, but without a true understanding of how to implement it effectively. (My own state of California came out with a shockingly bad take on this, to the point where free software like Linux could have been affected.) In the meantime, governments still have to figure out how they’ll direct the settlement funds, which will be paid over a 10-year period. And other lawsuits may introduce further changes for child use of social media: Additional cases from individuals, local governments, and school districts are pending in federal and state courts. (That includes Florida, which did not agree to the August 26 settlement.) But until the dust settles, I strongly recommend all adults get up to speed on digital dangers for teens—and then help the kids around us navigate them, same as we’d teach them for real-world concerns. Parents should take point in their children’s lives, but we’re all in this together. In the news This week was a reminder that sometimes, basic security goes a long way—when it’s in your control. Our privacy, on the other hand, is often in the hands of others…or, as illustrated by retailer AliExpress’s supposed shenanigans, purposely messed with. Retailer AliExpress allegedly is fingerprinting users through an older browser trick. AliExpress The good: Privacy-minded engineers have been fighting back against Meta glasses, creating apps to detect the hard-to-detect recording devices . The apps don’t fully combat the problem of secret recording, but they at least give a potential heads-up. The unexpected: Turns out Windows XP is still far more beloved than Windows 8 —according to Statcounter, it still holds a larger market share. Either way, this factoid is bad news if you’re on either operating system, as they’re no longer supported by security updates. Time to upgrade! The bad: ClarityCheck, a service that lets you look up people with a photo, exposed millions of images publicly —as well as email addresses and phone numbers. A sobering reminder that such data broker sites aren’t well-secured…and that you have little control over how someone can look you up online. Three UK airports leaked email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registration numbers, and postcodes of over 8 million travelers . Details were gathered by Manchester Airport, London Stansted, and East Midlands Airport through Wi-Fi use or airport bookings. Keep an eye out for phishing or scam attempts. Retailer AliExpress allegedly tracks users through silent audio played through browser tabs. Dan Goodwin of Ars Technica describes the technique as “outdated,” but I see it as proof that a simple approach can still get the job done. Close out your AliExpress browser tabs when you’re done, if you must shop there. Mini-PC maker Geekom admitted an outdated support page served malicious versions of its drivers. If you think you’ve been affected, wipe your PC and start again with a completely clean install of Windows—and to get your driver updates through Microsoft. Tip of the week Jinhan Moon / Unsplash Kids unfortunately can become targets for child exploitation—and AI tools have unfortunately made creation of sexually explicit, abusive content even easier. You can protect your kids by being careful about what you post online, especially as the school year starts. For starters, keep photos as private as possible. (I recommend sharing in group chats on secure chat apps, like Signal or WhatsApp.) Also, don’t share details about their birth dates, schools, or even preferences. Such information can be used by unscrupulous adults to groom children.

My plan right now is to possibly invest in a new workspace for my office, including the stylish, functional desk at the end of my list. This holder fits any laptop that’s between 0.47 and 1 inch think (from gaming to productivity devices), with a nice bit of cushy rubber to hold and protect your laptop. Ignore that Apple logo; it works with Windows laptops, too. View Deal SVNNELP Under Desk Drawer: $29.44 You’re always going to end up with little bits of stuff on your desk: staples, push pins, pens, cables, and more. How you deal with it is up to you, but one way is with an under-desk drawer. Amazon SVNNELP offers a trio of small, medium, and large desk drawers that you can pick and choose from. The kicker here is that they’re held on by strong adhesive, rather than screws. You can always opt for a more permanent screw-in model, but these sticky drawers work as long as you don’t store anything too heavy in them. View Deal OPNICE Desk Organizer: $21.99 One important point for desk organization that I mentioned earlier is to go vertical: A display that can be aligned vertical in portrait mode can improve a desk’s usable space. In this case, the OPNICE Desk Organizer is actually a monitor riser and a collection of bins to hold all of your extra stuff. Amazon If you’re like me, you raise your monitor up a bit via its stand or a riser. In this case, you’re using the extra space (20.5 x 9.5 x 6.3 inches) to good use. Sure, I’d lose a little space putting two Tribesigns in an L-shape, but the tradeoff is a generous amount of desktop, sufficient for an office setup as well as after-hours play space. It’s sturdy and supports up to 200 pounds; the desk itself weighs about 60 pounds. Also, it ships in a variety of finishes, from a neutral walnut finish to coffee and an oak-like stain. item.title: The Google Docs backup trick everybody should know
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Anyone who frequently writes documents has had that moment where a big edit goes sideways. So what do you do when you’ve deleted a paragraph you needed, rewrote half a document only to regret the whole thing, or opened a shared file and scratched your head, wondering who changed what? There’s no need to freak out. Google Docs has a safety net called “version history” that remembers every version of your work. To find it, open your document and go to File > Version history > See version history . You’ll see older drafts listed by date and time on the right side of the screen. You can click on any of them to preview how the document looked at that point. Google also shows who made changes, with different colors tied to different editors, which I find really helpful when several people are working in the same file as me. If you find the draft you want, click Restore this version , and Google Docs will replace your current document with that older draft. You can also make a separate copy of an older version if you only want to recover a section without replacing your current work. One habit I highly recommend is naming important versions before you make any major changes. Go to File > Version history > Name current version and give it a useful label such as “First draft” or “Final draft before edits.” Named versions are much easier to spot later, and Google even says naming a version also keeps it from being merged with other revisions later. It only takes a few seconds, but it can save you from the headaches of trying to remember your earlier brilliant idea before someone accidentally deleted it. They cost more, but provide more functionality. (A FAQ at the end of this roundup can help you decide.) I keep at least one of these lightweight little USB-C hubs in my backpack at all times. You should too! Why you should trust PCWorld for USB-C hub reviews and buying advice: PCWorld has been supplying news, reviews, and recommendations for the best computing products since our first magazines hit newsstand shelves in 1983. Mokin 160W GaN All in One Docking Station: Further considerations The split between data-only and charging ports is a little weird, especially if you’re using a mouse, keyboard, and webcam — and that extra USB-A port just isn’t available. (Really, who needs a power-only USB-A port?) But this dock pretty much nails your basic needs, offers a compact form factor, and is priced right, too. Read our full Mokin 160W GaN All in One Docking Station review Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615 – Best full-sized USB-C DisplayLink dock Pros Terrific price and value Excellent stability Great display port flexibility Support for two 4K60 displays Cons Have to provide your own power supply Can get quite warm Mandatory software driver Price When Reviewed: $169.99 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 23% off original price $129.99 View Deal $169.99 View Deal Ugreen $169.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Who should buy the Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615? DisplayLink docks fit between a USB-C dongle and a Thunderbolt dock, and I always think of a DisplayLink buyer as a small business owner or home worker who is focused on productivity and lots of high-end displays. DisplayLink docks excel for office work, but struggle in handling high frame rates for games. This is our top pick for an upgraded DisplayLink dock , which has its own pros and cons — slightly more expensive than a USB-C docking station, but more features, too. Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615: Further considerations Ugreen’s 9-in-1 USB-C docking station is typical of the brand: quality design and manufacture, obtuse naming, and pricing that seems to vary from one vendor to the next. But this DisplayLink dock offers an excellent mix of port flexibility at a solid price. There is one catch: It lacks any power input at all, and you’ll need to use your laptop’s USB-C power supply (or buy one) to charge both this dock and the laptop itself. Like most DisplayLink docks, this dock was unusually stable, with no flickering between displays — one of the reasons I like DisplayLink docks. The price nails that sweet spot, too. Just remember to bring your smartphone charger. Read our full Ugreen 9-in-1 USB-C (Revodok) Docking Station CM615 review Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ) – Best full-sized USB-C DisplayLink dock runner-up Pros Support for three 4K60 displays Six USB-A ports 60W of power Cons Great, stable image quality breaks down slightly with video No USB-C or fast-charging ports Price When Reviewed: $199.95 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price Check on Amazon Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Who should buy the Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ)? As noted in the best pick above, DisplayLink docks work best for a home office, with an emphasis on productivity. You’ll want to avoid gaming. Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ): Further considerations Plugable’s dock means that you can connect to three 4K displays, even if you don’t absolutely have to. Most docks ask you to choose between DisplayPort and HDMI, or even use a direct Thunderbolt connection. Plugable offers both. The performance of this dock was up to par, though keep in mind that DisplayLink uses compressed data running over a 10Gbps connection. Press it too hard, and you will see some degradation in video and storage performance. Read our full Plugable USB-C Triple 4K HDMI and DisplayPort Display Horizontal Docking Station (UD-6950PDZ) review Other USB-C hub/dock reviews and features Anker Nano 13-in-1 USB-C dock review: This combo USB-C dock/hub doesn’t deliver the amount of charging power I’d hope for, though the two-for-one special is unique. Mokin 160W GaN All-in-One Station : With great power comes great…performance. Ugreen’s $5 cable deal: Deals come and go, but check back for an attractive price. USB-C buying guide : Our friends at PCWelt have some advice on how to differentiate USB from Thunderbolt. How we test USB-C hubs We test USB-C hubs/dongles slightly differently than docking stations. A separate article offers a detailed explanation on how we test USB-C hubs , but here’s a short summary: First we test the physical configuration, and how ports are spaced and whether filling one port impedes use of the port next to it. We also run performance tests to make sure ports function as advertised. Finally, we consider price and weight it against functionality and build quality. More complex hubs usually command more money, but that’s not always the case! Who curated this article? My name is Mark Hachman , and I’ve been working as a technology reporter and reviewer for 30 years. I review USB-C hubs/dongles, Thunderbolt docking stations, and DisplayLink docks, so I have a good handle on the different types of I/O technologies being used and what will be best for you. I’ve been reviewing these devices since work-from-home became popular in 2020, realizing pretty quickly that home users wanted a mix of displays and legacy peripherals. How to choose the best USB-C hub You’ll want to do a careful of assessment of your work equipment and your needs in order to find the right hub or dock for yourself. First, take stock of your peripherals Here’s where to start: Take a look at the peripherals you own, or plan to buy. Do you have an old external hard drive that uses a traditional USB-A cable? Do you manually back up photos from an SLR camera via its SD card? Or is your Wi-Fi connection unreliable enough that you’d prefer Ethernet? Figure out what ports you’ll need. This advice is for Windows users; Macs have their own limitations on USB-C connections. Keep in mind that you may want to use both a mouse and keyboard, and possibly connect a printer, too. You can disconnect a keyboard to print, but it’s kind of a pain. Even if you own a modern 2026 laptop, you may still have hardware from several years ago. A hub bridges your laptop to its peripherals, but can serve as a bridge to the past, too. This laptop has several USB-C ports, but if yours has just one, you’ll want to daisy-chain the laptop’s power cord by plugging it directly into the hub, like so. Next, check out what ports your laptop already has It’s also important to take stock of your laptop or tablet’s ports: Does it have one USB-C port or two? If your device only has one port, is there a separate charging connection? If your laptop or tablet has a USB-C port and uses it exclusively for charging , you’ll want to buy a USB-C hub with a dedicated charging input port. Note how much input power the port allows, and confirm that it will be sufficient for your laptop. Otherwise, you’ll be forced to choose between charging your laptop and accessing other devices, which makes little sense. Most laptops will pop up a warning about a “slow charger” if your laptop’s not getting enough juice. A laptop’s USB-C port. Matt Smith/IDG Video adds another wrinkle. Older laptops often included dedicated video ports, often HDMI; modern laptops in 2026 may include a dedicated video port as well. But video can also run over the USB-C port through a technology called DP Alt Mode which enables certain USB-C ports to send video signals to external monitors using the DisplayPort protocol, via the USB-C cable. The problem, even as manufacturers like BenQ admit , is that these cables aren’t often properly labeled. There’s no way for us to tell you whether your USB-C port can support video passing over it. You’ll need to consult your laptop’s manual to tell. If the port does support video, you can either use a USB-C hub to connect to an external monitor. Alternatively, you can run the USB-C cable to a display with a USB-C cable input. These USB-C displays have only been available for a few years, but they provide an alternate way of routing video out of your laptop. Assess your laptop and peripheral power needs Desktop hubs will often take power in from an external charger like the one you plug into your phone, and use it to power your laptop. On these hubs or dongles, there will be a dedicated USB-C input port to accept power, but not data. A powered laptop docking station, on the other hand, ships with its own charger — which may be hardwired into the docking station and take will power in and also push it out to peripherals. As I noted above, the input power to your laptop needs to be sufficient to power it. But if you’re investing in a powered USB-C docking station, check our reviews to see how much power the hub or docking station can push out to peripherals. The 2026 iPhone 17 Max consumes 40W of charging power to fast-charge the phone; most docking stations won’t get near that. But an older phone, such as an Apple iPhone 14, only needed 30W of charging power. Older phones need even less power to fast-charge them. You certainly don’t have to buy a USB-C docking station or hub to charge a phone; most hubs weren’t built with them in mind. It’s useful to know, however, what your hub or docking station will be able to do or not do. Making sense of the USB-C technologies A USB-C port on your laptop can either run at 5Gbps or 10Gbps, with the latter being almost ubiquitous these days. That’s plenty of bandwidth for a printer, a mouse, a keyboard, or a hard drive, even all at once. Products like displays, Ethernet, and high-speed SSDs gobble up that bandwidth, however. Display technologies tend to have the most influence over what you should buy. If you simply want to connect to an external 1080p display — or two — a USB-C dongle should work fine, provided that the dongle has the available ports. It’s certainly the cheapest option. If you want to connect more displays with higher resolution, you may have to examine other choices. Traditionally, the only other alternative was a Thunderbolt dock . Provided your laptop had a Thunderbolt port, Thunderbolt’s 40Gbps bandwidth allows for two 4K displays, running at 60Hz, plus various peripherals. (You can use a 10Gbps USB-C dock even if you have a 40Gbps Thunderbolt port, but only 10Gbps of that throughput will be available to the 10Gbps dock.) Thunderbolt is usually associated with laptops which use Intel processors; laptops with AMD Ryzen or Qualcomm Snapdragon chips inside use the “generic” equivalent, also called USB4. There are also two intermediary technologies to choose from: a DisplayLink USB-C dock, and a USB-C dock that takes advantage of something called HBR3 and DSC. DisplayLink , owned by Synaptics, uses software compression between your laptop and the dock to approximate a Thunderbolt experience over a generic USB-C connection. It requires a software driver, but our experience is that it’s an excellent choice for office work, but not gaming. Here are the best DisplayLink docks and why to buy them. HBR3 with Display Compression ( HBR3 with DSC ) is essentially an industry standard version of DisplayLink. The problem? The technology hasn’t been widely publicized, let alone supported. Our experience has been that docks that support HBR3 work well with laptops using 12th-gen Core processors on up. Laptops with a 10th-gen Core chip inside them aren’t supported, and 11th-gen Core laptops are iffy. If you own a laptop chip with a 12th-gen Core chip or one that’s even more recent, you stand a good chance of success. Otherwise, don’t bother. Thunderbolt cables and ports include the little lightning-bolt icon, which differentiates them from the otherwise unmarked USB-C cables. Finally, don’t worry about platform branding Because USB-C is common among Macs, Windows PCs, and phones, some hubs align their branding with a particular platform. Go ahead and use that USB-C that’s billed as being “for MacBook Pro, Chromebook, and XPS” with any Windows PC — we did, and it works just fine. You won’t need any special software or drivers. After testing our USB-C hubs, we can confirm that some no-names perform just as well as their more well-known counterparts, and for less money, too. One thing to keep in mind: Because price is so critical to our recommendations, know that some of the prices may change as manufacturers offer sales. Therefore some hubs we didn’t recommend primarily based on price could become more purchase-worthy. FAQ 1. Why buy a USB-C hub or dongle? Remember when laptops used to contain all sorts of ports: USB-A, HDMI, SD card slots, and more? And do you remember how svelte the early Macintosh laptops looked, especially when Apple began removing all of the ports in favor of USB-C and Thunderbolt? PC makers did, and decided that was the approach that they would take, too. Unfortunately, that left laptop owners like you with the problem of legacy hardware: printers, keyboards, SD card, micro SD cards, and so on — and with no ports to plug them into. Enter the USB-C hub, an inexpensive product that helps solve that problem. Just pay attention to what ports the USB-C hub offers, to make sure it meets your needs. 2. I don’t understand what the difference is between a USB-C hub, a DisplayLink dock, and a Thunderbolt docking station. What do I need? Here’s the short answer: If you want to connect your laptop to a printer, an SD card or microSD card, mouse, keyboard, or legacy 1080p monitor, stick with a basic 10Gbps USB-C hub/dongle. If you want to add a pair of additional displays (especially 4K), or high-speed SSD drives, we’d recommend you look at our list of 40Gbps Thunderbolt docking stations . Generally, the larger, powered docks offer more features. It is confusing, since they all use the “same” USB-C port. Generally, most modern laptops have a small Thunderbolt “lightning bolt” logo to help distinguish the faster port. 3. What’s the difference between a USB-C hub, USB-C dongle, and a USB-C docking station? A USB-C hub or dongle (we use the terms interchangeably) is a small, portable device that you can slide into a bag or backpack. A USB-C docking station tends to be heavy and bulky enough that you’ll want to keep it on your desk. It’s not true that a USB-C docking station will have more features than a USB-C hub, as some compact USB-C hubs pack in a surprising number of ports. Docking stations tend to be bigger and bulkier, and are designed to live on your desk. If there’s anything that docking stations tend to have that dongles sometimes don’t, it’s a USB-C port designed only to accept power from your laptop’s USB-C charger. That allows you to gain additional ports as well as charging capabilities from the same dock. 4. How much does a USB-C hub or dongle cost? Expect to pay between $30 and $40 for a good USB-C hub, even in 2026 — maybe a bit more with tariffs. USB-C docking stations are bigger and bulkier but add even more capabilities. We’d expect you to pay over $100 for these. 5. How much does price matter when buying a USB-C hub or dongle? Honestly, not much. Pay attention to our reviews and those from other shoppers, but buy according to what the hub or dongle offers. You can absolutely find solid USB-C hubs and dongles for an inexpensive price. USB-C docking stations , though, can feel a bit overpriced. In part, that’s because Thunderbolt docks were wildly expensive during the 2020 to 2021 pandemic years. USB-C docking stations are an alternative, but their prices were nudged upward, too. Fortunately, prices have come down, as the supply chain regained a semblance of normalcy. 6. What is the difference between USB-C and Thunderbolt? Both USB-C and Thunderbolt use the same USB-C connection. The difference is that a “generic” USB-C connection typically provides 10Gbps of bandwidth, and Thunderbolt provides 40Gbps, or 120Gbps with Thunderbolt 5 . Thunderbolt ports are becoming much more common, so it’s possible that your laptop won’t have any “USB-C” ports; they’ll be Thunderbolt-enabled instead. (To tell the difference, consult your laptop’s manual or look for a small “lightning bolt” logo over the port itself. That’s usually a sign that it’s a Thunderbolt port.) A USB-C dongle and a Thunderbolt dock are similar, in that they both provide a number of additional ports. There’s a key difference, though. The rule of thumb is that a USB-C dongle provides enough bandwidth for two 1080p displays at 60Hz, or a single 4K display at 30Hz. (Staring at any 30Hz display for a length of time can tire out your eyes, so I don’t recommend it.) A Thunderbolt dock, however, allows enough bandwidth to connect two 4K displays at 60Hz, plus all the peripherals you wish to attach. If you don’t need big, high-resolution displays, don’t buy a Thunderbolt dock and purchase a USB-C hub instead. 7. What’s a DisplayLink USB-C dock? A DisplayLink USB-C dock is what you might call a “tweener” device: something between USB-C and Thunderbolt. DisplayLink docks embed a small chip from Synaptics in the docking station, and require use of a software driver that you’ll need to download. (USB-C and Thunderbolt are essentially plug and play.) The Synaptics chip compresses the data, and gives you the ability to connect (no joke) up to three or sometimes four 4K display all over a 10Gbps USB-C cable. It feels a bit like black magic. They’re not foolproof; DisplayLink docks are best for office work (email, Word, Excel, and so on that don’t require a whole lot of bandwidth, because the images are largely static) and web browsing. Transfer a lot of data (or play back a lot of high-bitrate video) and you’ll see some stuttering. We used to break out DisplayLink docks into their own page, but we now include recommendations on this list of the best USB-C hubs, as well as our list of the best Thunderbolt docks . If you shop smart, you can get the capabilities of a Thunderbolt dock, for less. 8. Can you connect a USB-C dongle to a Thunderbolt dock? Or to another USB-C hub? You can absolutely connect a USB-C hub to a Thunderbolt dock. You probably won’t be able to connect a USB-C dongle to another USB-C dongle/hub, but if your laptop has more than one USB-C port, you can connect a USB-C hub to each. Thunderbolt offers the ability to “daisy-chain” devices, however, so you can connect one Thunderbolt dock to another. USB-C, however, does not. 9. Why do USB-C hubs get so hot? USB-C hubs can get warm or even hot while using them to transfer data or charge devices. This is because the electronic components and circuitry within hubs build up heat during use. Depending upon the hub’s material, heat can become trapped inside the hub leading it to become hot to the touch. If you are concerned about your hub becoming too hot during use, you may consider purchasing a hub made from metallic parts, such as aluminum, so that heat can more easily dissipate as it builds up. Even though two USB-C hubs may have wildly different brand names, you may sometimes find that they’re otherwise identical or just very similar. We’ve given you a lot of detail on what makes a good USB-C hub or dongle and what to consider when buying one. In general, however, these are fairly inexpensive, flexible ways to upgrade your laptop, and I’d recommend always carrying one in your laptop bag!

item.title: 14 clever USB-C gadgets I’d actually keep in my tech drawer
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
I don’t know how your tech drawers look, but mine are filled with wires I’ll likely never use again because technology has advanced quite a bit. Thankfully, USB-C seems to be here to stay since there is no wrong way to plug these things in. It’s not just smartphones, tablets, and laptops that use these, however, but also a long list of gadgets. We’ve scoured the market for hidden gems: 14 gadgets that will make you think “Wow, I didn’t know I needed that, but it will make my life so much easier!” Let’s dive in and see what cool devices you’ll be able to use your type-C cables and ports with. Unihand rechargeable hand warmers Unihand As the weather is getting colder, you sometimes wish you could warm up your hands a bit faster. Well, these $20 hand warmers are rechargeable and perfectly ready to keep your fingers toasty for up to 20 hours on a single charge. These gadgets feature a temperature sensor chip that helps you pick one of three temps for precise control. There are plenty of colors to choose from, too. Firrax 74-in-1 mini electric screwdriver If you often have to fiddle around with your computer or other gadgets, this Firrax mini electric screwdriver kit may be just what you need. This pen-shaped screwdriver features three LED lights so it’s easier to see what you’re working on. The screwdriver has a stylish base so you can hold it on your desk, and a whole collection of 64 S2 steel bits. The screwdriver can be charged via USB-C and it can last for hours — the manufacturer says it can drive over 500 screws before needing a recharge. This super fun electric screwdriver usually goes for $36, but can often be found on sale. Anker Nano Power Bank Anker One thing you need to have in you bag/pocket/backpack is a power bank because you never really know when your phone will fail you and cry for a recharge. Well, the Anker Nano power bank is tiny enough to fit just about anywhere. It comes with a foldable USB-C connector and a port on the side so you can charge two devices at once if you need to. The 5,000mAh capacity is just about enough for a full phone recharge, so it will be great in a pinch. It’s also only $27. Endoscope camera with light Although it’s not something you’ll use every day, this USB-C endoscope camera can definitely come in handy. You just plug it in your phone, install and app, and see everything your camera does. Our team swears by it , using it for finding whatever they dropped behind the desk, while working on the car, or looking for pipe leaks. Since it has an IP67 rating , you can even plop it in your aquarium. The camera comes with a 16.4ft semi-rigid cable and several accessories, including a hook, magnet, and a mirror. You can get this one for $60 or less. Blukar flashlight Blukar I don’t care who you are—you need a flashlight. The smaller, the better, because you get to shove it into any pocket. This model from Blukar comes with a built-in 1800mAh battery that you’ll recharge with one of those many type-C cables you have in that tech drawer we were talking about. It can work for up to 16 hours on a single charge, which is pretty decent. There are four different lightning modes to cycle through, including one that will help you signal for help. Plus, one of these is just $9, so no excuse to pass on this one. Heat It insect bite healer Anyone plagued by mosquitoes in the summer will be particularly pleased with this ingenious gadget. This tiny device, which can be easily connected to your smartphone via USB-C, can significantly reduce the itching of bites and stings with targeted heat. You simply charge the small Heat It bite healer via the app and then hold it on the bite. The heat then does the rest, breaking down the proteins in the mosquito bite that cause the area to swell, itch, and hurt. A true must-have for summer, and it costs only $30. A tiny air pump Also perfect for summer is this small air pump from Cycplus , which fits in any bag while on the go. Not only can it inflate a bicycle tire in two minutes at the touch of a button, but it’s also USB-charged. According to the manufacturer, it’s suitable for mountain bikes, road bikes, motorcycles, and even cars! In addition to being an air pump, this practical gadget can also be used as a flashlight or power bank for on-the-go use — all things that come in very handy on a bike ride. And at just $36, it’s highly recommended if you need quick help with a flat tire. USB-C mini fan These little fans are also pretty ingenious; you can easily carry them in your pocket in the summer and quickly use them whenever you need them. Anyone who’s ever sat on a crowded subway train in 30-degree heat and wished for at least a little fresh air will love this gadget. The mini fan, which costs just $16 , has a USB-C port and can be easily powered by power banks, computers, laptops, or USB chargers. There are even smaller and cheaper fans available that can be connected directly to your phone, costing under $10 each. But these also provide less powerful airflow, so we recommend the standalone version. Reading light with a book clamp Anyone who enjoys reading a lot, sometimes late into the night, will appreciate this little gadget: a reading lamp that you can simply clip onto your book. It may not be groundbreaking, but with a total of three color temperatures and five different light modes, you can individually adjust how much light you need for reading. The Gritin reading lamp costs just $9 on Amazon and features a 1200 mAh battery that lasts up to 80 hours depending on usage. Afterward, you can easily recharge it via USB. You can swivel the neck of the lamp back and forth as desired, and there’s even a small charging indicator. What more could you want? External DVD Drive Amicool If your laptop is like mine and lacks a DVD drive, then this little gadget will come in handy for you. This Amicool external DVD drive uses a USB-C (or USB-A) to connect to your laptop and give yout he optical drive you sometimes need. It can read and burn DVDs and CDs with ease, allowing you to install software, copy files, back up data, play games, and so on. You won’t even need to install drives as this thing is plug and play. While this thing’s usually $29, you can often get it for around $20, which is an absolute bargain. Type-C microSD card reader Ugreen Most laptops nowadays don’t come with a card reader anymore (I know mine doesn’t), so finding other ways to get data off those little buggers is a must. Whether you need to pull data off your dashcam’s card or if it’s from your camera, this tiny Ugreen USB-C microSD reader will work just fine. This reader is tiny enough that you should probably put it on a keychain of some kind. If you’d rather a slightly more versatile version, Ugreen has a model that also works with SD cards and features both USB-C and USB-A connectors. Any of these will cost you less than $10, so they’re worthwhile investments. USB-C to HDMI adapter Anker If your laptop has a USB-C port but you haven’t updated your monitor in ages, your display won’t feature a Type-C port. This Anker adapter fixes this problem for you, enabling you to connect the regular HDMI cable you plug in your monitor with this gadget. The adapter supports resolutions of up to 4K at 60Hz, which is pretty awesome. This is also a nifty way to connect your phone or tablet to your monitor or TV. This thing’s $17. Electric Air Duster Wolfbox This tiny little thing is going to be such a useful gadget to have. Despite its size, it has quite a lot of power and you can use it easily to clean up crumbs from your keyboard and the dust from your PC tower, clean the vents in your car or the dryer lint trap, for instance — it’s great to use every once in a while. You can also use this tiny gadget to inflate mattresses when camping or your kid’s floaties. The best part is that you can use a regular USB-C cord to recharge it. This Wolfbox MF100 electric air duster is usually $90, but you can get it on sale quite often. Measuring Tools Hoto This pocket-sized laser measuring tool will make your life so much easier because it’s sooooo compact. Whenever you take on any DIY projects, whether it’s anything serious or you’re just putting up a painting, this laser measuring tool will be useful. It has two measuring modes, it’s quite accurate, and features a hidden OLED display that tells you exactly what it measures and the battery life. It even comes with Bluetooth so you can record more data after connecting it to your phone. And of course, you can charge it with a USB-C cable. This Hoto tool is usually $45 , but we’ve seen it on sale for closer to $30 quite often, especially if you have a Prime subscription. Editor’s note: This article was originally published on May 16, 2025, but was updated to include additional devices.
